title: Signal Processing
subtitle: Sampling, convolution, the Fourier transform, filters and windows, with runnable Python labs and a spectrum lab
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A hands-on introduction to digital signal processing: signals and systems, sampling, aliasing and quantisation, convolution and impulse responses, the discrete Fourier transform and FFT, FIR and IIR filters with frequency response and the z-transform, windows and spectral leakage, and applications in noise removal, pitch detection, decimation, image filtering and compression. Every chapter has Python labs verified in the built-in interpreter, and two interactive labs let you explore aliasing and filtering with live spectra.

chapters.title: Signals and systems: what we are processing

maps.title: Signals
links: Analog signal | is | Continuous in time
Digital signal | is | Sampled and quantised

summary: A signal is a quantity that varies, usually with time, and carries information: sound pressure, a heartbeat voltage, a stock price, the brightness along a row of pixels. A system takes a signal in and produces a signal out.
Analog signals are continuous. Digital signal processing (DSP) works on lists of numbers that were sampled at regular steps, which computers can handle exactly.
The simplest signal is the sine wave, described by amplitude, frequency and phase. Almost every other signal can be built from sines.

glossary.def: A function that carries information, such as a value that changes with time.
Anything that turns an input signal into an output signal.
The size of a signal's swing.
How many cycles happen per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
How far a wave is shifted along the time axis.

keyPoints: A sine: A sin(2 pi f t + phase).
Period T = 1 / f.
Digital signals are lists of numbers.
A system maps input signals to output signals.
Every real signal can be built from sines.

items: ELI5. A sound is wiggles in the air. A computer writes down the height of the wiggle again and again, and that list of numbers is a digital signal.

Look at a voice recorded on a phone. Behind the file is a list of numbers, thousands per second, each one the air pressure at a moment. That list is a digital signal. Signal processing is the art of changing, cleaning and understanding such lists.

The sine wave is the building block. Its three numbers are amplitude, how tall it is; frequency, how many times it repeats per second; and phase, where in its cycle it starts. A 440 hertz sine with amplitude one sounds as the note A above middle C.

The period is the time for one cycle, and equals one divided by the frequency. A 100 hertz wave repeats every 0.01 seconds. Signals made of several sines add up, and the sum can look complicated while each part is simple.

A system is anything that acts on signals: an amplifier, an echo, a filter, a microphone. Some systems are linear and time-invariant, called LTI systems. They have a beautiful theory built on convolution and Fourier analysis, which is the core of this course.
Along the way we will use Python to build signals, sample them, filter them and look at their spectra. The same ideas run inside phones, radios, medical scanners, music software and radar.

practice.title: Period from frequency
practice.intro: Write period(f): the period in seconds of a sine of frequency f hertz, 1 / f, rounded to 6 decimals.
practice.hint: One divided by f.
practice.solution:
def period(f):
    return round(1.0 / f, 6)

practice.title: Generate a sine
practice.intro: Write sine(amp, freq, phase, fs, n): the first n samples of amp x sin(2 pi freq t + phase) sampled at fs samples per second (t = k / fs). Return the list of samples multiplied by 1000 and rounded to integers, so that the values are exact to compare.
practice.hint: Loop over sample numbers k and compute the time k over fs.
practice.solution:
import math
def sine(amp, freq, phase, fs, n):
    out = []
    for k in range(n):
        v = amp * math.sin(2 * math.pi * freq * k / fs + phase)
        out.append(int(round(v * 1000)))
    return out

practice.title: Sum of two sines
practice.intro: Write mix(f1, f2, fs, n): the first n samples of sin(2 pi f1 t) + sin(2 pi f2 t) at sample rate fs, multiplied by 1000 and rounded to integers.
practice.hint: Add the two sines at each time.
practice.solution:
import math
def mix(f1, f2, fs, n):
    out = []
    for k in range(n):
        t = k / float(fs)
        v = math.sin(2 * math.pi * f1 * t) + math.sin(2 * math.pi * f2 * t)
        out.append(int(round(v * 1000)))
    return out

chapters.title: Sampling, aliasing and quantisation

maps.title: Sampling
links: Sample rate | is | Samples per second
Nyquist | needs | Twice the top frequency
Bit depth | sets | Number of levels

summary: To store a continuous signal in a computer we sample it: measure it at regular instants. The sample rate fs is how many samples per second we take.

The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem says that a signal containing no frequency above B can be captured perfectly if fs is more than 2B. Sampling too slowly causes aliasing: a high frequency masquerades as a lower one.
Each sample is also rounded to one of a finite number of levels, called quantisation. With b bits there are 2^b levels, and the rounding error behaves like a faint noise.

glossary.def: The number of samples taken per second.
Half the sample rate; the highest frequency that can be represented.
The false appearance of a high frequency as a lower one when sampled too slowly.
Rounding each sample to the nearest of a finite set of levels.
The number of bits per sample; b bits give 2^b levels.

keyPoints: Sample faster than 2 times the top frequency.
Nyquist frequency = fs / 2.
Alias of f: fold into 0..fs/2.
CD audio: 44100 Hz, 16 bits.
6 dB of range per bit.

items: ELI5. If a camera takes pictures too slowly, a spinning wheel looks like it turns the wrong way. Sampling too slowly makes fast wiggles look slow.

Imagine filming a spinning wheel. If the camera takes too few pictures per second, the wheel can seem to turn slowly, or even backwards. That is aliasing. The camera sampled too slowly to follow the true motion, and the samples fit a slower false story.

The rule is the sampling theorem. If the highest frequency in a signal is B, sample at more than twice B. Human hearing reaches about 20,000 hertz, so CD audio uses 44,100 samples per second. Half of that, 22,050 hertz, is the Nyquist frequency.

What if a frequency above the Nyquist frequency sneaks in? It folds back. A 30 hertz sine sampled at 40 hertz appears as a 10 hertz sine, because 40 minus 30 is 10. To prevent this, real systems put an analog anti-aliasing filter before the sampler to remove frequencies above the limit.
Sampling is only half of digitising. Each sample must be stored with a limited number of bits. This is quantisation. With 3 bits there are 8 levels. With 16 bits, as on a CD, there are 65,536 levels.
The difference between the true value and the rounded one acts like a small noise, and each extra bit improves the signal-to-noise ratio by about 6 decibels.

Choosing rates and bit depths is an engineering trade-off. Speech needs only about 8,000 samples per second. Music needs 44,100 or more. Medical and scientific systems may need many more bits. The labs let you compute aliases and quantise signals yourself.

chapters.title: Discrete systems and convolution

maps.title: Systems
links: LTI system | is | Linear and time-invariant

summary: A discrete system turns an input list x[n] into an output list y[n]. If it is linear (outputs add and scale with inputs) and time-invariant (shifting the input shifts the output), it is an LTI system.
Feed an LTI system a single impulse, a 1 followed by zeros, and the output is its impulse response h[n]. Every other output is then the convolution of the input with h.
Convolution slides a flipped copy of h along x, multiplying and adding, and it is the main operation of filtering.

glossary.def: A signal that is 1 at n = 0 and 0 elsewhere.
The output of a system when the input is an impulse, written h[n].
The operation y[n] = sum over k of x[k] h[n - k].
A system whose outputs add and scale with inputs and do not depend on when the input starts.
A filter whose impulse response has finite length.

keyPoints: y[n] = sum of x[k] h[n - k].
Length of x * h = len(x) + len(h) - 1.
Convolution is commutative and associative.
Convolving with an impulse leaves a signal unchanged.
A delay is convolution with a shifted impulse.

items: ELI5. A system is a machine that changes a signal. Poke it once and watch what comes out, and you learn how it treats every signal.

Take a simple system: it outputs the average of the current input and the previous one. Give it a single 1 followed by zeros. The output is half, half, zero. That output is the impulse response, and it fully describes the system.

Why? Any input is a sum of scaled and shifted impulses. A linear time-invariant system turns each impulse into a scaled, shifted copy of the impulse response. Adding them up gives the output. That sum is the convolution of the input with the impulse response.

To compute it by hand, flip the impulse response, slide it along the input, and at each position multiply overlapping numbers and add. The output has length of x plus length of h minus one. In code it is a double loop: for each input sample and each tap, add the product to the right output position.

An FIR filter, finite impulse response, has an impulse response that ends. A moving average is a typical example. An IIR filter, infinite impulse response, uses feedback so that the response never quite stops, like the echo of a shout in a canyon. Chapters on filters will build both.

Convolution has handy properties. It is commutative and associative, so cascading two filters gives the same result in either order. Convolving with a single impulse changes nothing, and convolving with a delayed impulse delays the signal. Echo effects in audio are convolution with a few spikes.

chapters.title: The Fourier idea and the DFT
summary: Fourier's idea is that any signal can be written as a sum of sine waves of different frequencies, amplitudes and phases. The spectrum shows how much of each frequency a signal contains.

The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) turns N samples into N complex numbers, one for each frequency bin. Bin k corresponds to the frequency k fs / N. The magnitude of the bin tells how strong that frequency is.
The fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes the same result in about N log N steps instead of N squared, which made digital spectrum analysis practical.

glossary.def: A description of a signal's strength at each frequency.
The discrete Fourier transform: X[k] = sum over n of x[n] e^(-2 pi i k n / N).
One output of the DFT, covering a narrow band of frequency.
The spacing between bins, fs / N.
A fast algorithm for the DFT, taking about N log N operations.

keyPoints: X[k] = sum x[n] (cos - i sin)(2 pi k n / N).
Bin k is at k fs / N hertz.
Real signal: bins above N/2 mirror the lower ones.
Magnitude = sqrt(re^2 + im^2).
Resolution = fs / N.

items: ELI5. A chord is many notes at once. The Fourier transform listens and tells you which notes are in it and how loud each is.

A musical chord sounds like one thing, but your ear can pick out the notes. The Fourier transform does the same for numbers. Give it a list of samples, and it says how much of each pure frequency the list contains.

The recipe for the DFT is simple. For each frequency bin k, multiply the signal by a cosine and a sine that complete k cycles over the N samples, and add up the results. If the signal contains that frequency, the products line up and the sum is large. If not, they cancel and the sum is small.

The cosine sum gives the real part and the minus sine sum gives the imaginary part. The magnitude, the square root of their squares, is the strength of the frequency. The angle gives its phase. To plot a spectrum, you usually plot the magnitude against frequency.

Bin k stands for the frequency k times fs divided by N. If you sample at 1000 hertz and take 100 samples, the bins are 10 hertz apart. A real signal has a mirror-image spectrum, so only bins up to N over two carry new information, up to the Nyquist frequency.

Computing the DFT directly takes N squared multiplications. The fast Fourier transform, popularised by Cooley and Tukey in 1965, splits the sum into even and odd samples and reuses work, getting N log N. For a million samples that is the difference between hours and a fraction of a second.

practice.title: DFT magnitude
practice.intro: Write dft_mag(x): the magnitude |X[k]| of the DFT of the real list x for k = 0 to N-1, each value rounded to 3 decimals. Use X[k] = sum over n of x[n] (cos(2 pi k n / N) - i sin(2 pi k n / N)), so |X[k]| = sqrt(re^2 + im^2).
practice.hint: Two nested loops, summing cos and sin terms.
practice.solution:
import math
def dft_mag(x):
    n = len(x)
    out = []
    for k in range(n):
        re = 0.0
        im = 0.0
        for t in range(n):
            ang = 2 * math.pi * k * t / n
            re = re + x[t] * math.cos(ang)
            im = im - x[t] * math.sin(ang)
        out.append(round(math.sqrt(re * re + im * im), 2))
    return out

practice.title: Bin frequency
practice.intro: Write bin_freq(k, fs, n): the centre frequency in hertz of DFT bin k for n samples at sample rate fs, k x fs / n, rounded to 3 decimals.
practice.hint: Multiply by fs and divide by n.
practice.solution:
def bin_freq(k, fs, n):
    return round(k * fs / float(n), 3)

practice.title: Peak frequency
practice.intro: Write peak_freq(x, fs): the frequency in hertz of the strongest bin among bins 1 to n//2 of the DFT of the real list x (skip bin 0, the average), computed with the DFT magnitudes. Return the frequency k x fs / n for the first bin with the largest magnitude.
practice.hint: Compute the magnitude for each bin and keep the largest.
practice.solution:
import math
def peak_freq(x, fs):
    n = len(x)
    best = 1
    bm = -1.0
    for k in range(1, n // 2 + 1):
        re = 0.0
        im = 0.0
        for t in range(n):
            ang = 2 * math.pi * k * t / n
            re = re + x[t] * math.cos(ang)
            im = im - x[t] * math.sin(ang)
        m = math.sqrt(re * re + im * im)
        if m > bm + 1e-9:
            bm = m
            best = k
    return best * fs / float(n)

chapters.title: FIR filters and frequency response

maps.title: FIR filters
links: Frequency response | is | Gain per frequency

summary: A filter changes how strongly each frequency is passed. A low-pass filter keeps low frequencies and removes high ones; a high-pass does the opposite; a band-pass keeps a range.
An FIR filter computes each output as a weighted sum of recent inputs, using a list of coefficients called taps. The moving average is the simplest low-pass.
The frequency response shows the gain at each frequency. For taps b it is H(w) = sum of b[k] e^(-i w k), and its magnitude tells how much of frequency w gets through.

glossary.def: A filter that passes low frequencies and attenuates high ones.
How a system's gain and phase change with frequency.
One coefficient of an FIR filter, multiplying one delayed sample.
The frequency where the gain starts to fall.
A filter with symmetric taps delays all frequencies equally.

keyPoints: H(w) = sum b[k] e^(-i w k).
Symmetric taps give linear phase.
Moving average: low-pass.
Difference [1, -1]: high-pass.

items: ELI5. A filter is like a sieve for sound: it lets the slow wiggles through and holds back the fast ones, or the other way round.

Imagine a smudge on a photograph that blends each pixel with its neighbours. A rapidly changing detail gets blurred away, while broad shapes remain. A low-pass filter does this to a signal along time.

The moving average over four samples is a low-pass FIR filter with taps one quarter, one quarter, one quarter, one quarter. A slow wave passes almost untouched because neighbouring samples are alike. A rapid wiggle averages to nearly zero because neighbours cancel.

The frequency response tells this precisely. Put the filter taps through the same sort of sum as the DFT: H of w equals the sum of b of k times e to the minus i w k. Its magnitude as a function of w is the gain curve. At w equal to zero it is just the sum of the taps.

Flip the sign of alternate taps and low-pass becomes high-pass. The two-tap filter one, minus one subtracts the previous sample, so it passes changes and removes steady levels. This is also a basic edge detector in images.

Designing a filter means choosing taps to approximate a desired gain curve. A classic method, the windowed sinc, takes the ideal low-pass impulse response, a sinc function, and tapers it with a window. Longer filters have sharper edges but cost more computation and delay.

chapters.title: IIR filters, feedback and the z-transform

maps.title: IIR filters
links: Stability | needs | Poles inside the circle
Transfer function | is | B over A

summary: An IIR filter feeds past outputs back into the calculation, y[n] = b0 x[n] - a1 y[n-1] and so on. It can achieve a sharp response with very few coefficients but has an impulse response that never exactly ends.
The z-transform turns a difference equation into algebra. The transfer function H(z) is a ratio of polynomials. Zeros are roots of the top, poles are roots of the bottom.
A causal filter is stable when every pole lies inside the unit circle, meaning |z| < 1. A pole on or outside the circle makes the output grow without bound.

glossary.def: A filter that feeds back its own past outputs, so its impulse response is infinite.
The ratio H(z) = B(z) / A(z) describing a filter in the z domain.
A value of z that makes the denominator of H(z) zero.
A value of z that makes the numerator of H(z) zero.
A system whose output stays bounded for bounded input.

keyPoints: y[n] = a x[n] + (1 - a) y[n-1] smooths.
Pole of 1 - p z^-1 is z = p.
Stable if all |poles| < 1.
Poles near the unit circle give sharp resonance.
Zeros on the unit circle null a frequency.

items: ELI5. Some filters listen to their own echo. That can make a lovely ring, but if the echo grows each time, the sound runs away.

Think of a bath tap and drain. The water level this minute depends on the level a minute ago plus what the tap adds. That feedback is an IIR filter. It forgets the past gradually, never quite all at once.

The simplest one is a one-pole low-pass: each output is a blend of the new input and the previous output, y of n equals a times x of n plus one minus a times y of n minus one. Small a means heavy smoothing and slow response.
It is used everywhere to calm noisy sensor readings, because it needs just one stored number.
The z-transform replaces delays by powers of z to the minus one. Then the filter becomes a fraction, H of z equals B of z over A of z.
Roots of the denominator are the poles, and they decide the character of the filter: where they sit tells whether it rings, how fast it decays, and whether it is stable.

The stability rule is clean. A causal filter is stable when all poles are strictly inside the unit circle. The pole of the one-pole filter is at one minus a. With a between zero and one it lies inside. With a bigger than two it lies outside, and the output explodes.

Compared with FIR, IIR filters are cheaper for a given sharpness, but they are harder to make linear-phase and can be unstable or noisy in fixed-point arithmetic. A common safe design splits high-order filters into small second-order sections called biquads.

practice.title: One-pole smoother
practice.intro: Write smooth(x, a): y[n] = a x[n] + (1 - a) y[n-1], with y[-1] = 0 (so y[0] = a x[0]). Return the list rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.hint: Keep the previous output in a variable.
practice.solution:
def smooth(x, a):
    y = []
    prev = 0.0
    for v in x:
        prev = a * v + (1 - a) * prev
        y.append(round(prev, 4))
    return y

practice.title: Step response
practice.intro: Write iir_impulse(a1, n): the first n samples of the impulse response of y[k] = x[k] - a1 y[k-1] (input 1, 0, 0, ...). Round each to 4 decimals.
practice.hint: Feed the previous output back with a minus sign.
practice.solution:
def iir_impulse(a1, n):
    out = []
    prev = 0.0
    for k in range(n):
        xk = 1.0 if k == 0 else 0.0
        prev = xk - a1 * prev
        out.append(round(prev, 4))
    return out

practice.title: Is it stable?
practice.intro: Write stable(a1): for the filter y[n] = x[n] - a1 y[n-1], return True if the pole z = -a1 lies strictly inside the unit circle, otherwise False.
practice.hint: Compare the pole's magnitude with 1.
practice.solution:
def stable(a1):
    return abs(-a1) < 1

practice.title: Biquad run
practice.intro: Write biquad(x, b0, b1, b2, a1, a2): the direct form I filter y[n] = b0 x[n] + b1 x[n-1] + b2 x[n-2] - a1 y[n-1] - a2 y[n-2], with zeros before the start. Return rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.hint: Remember two past inputs and two past outputs.
practice.solution:
def biquad(x, b0, b1, b2, a1, a2):
    y = []
    x1 = 0.0
    x2 = 0.0
    y1 = 0.0
    y2 = 0.0
    for v in x:
        out = b0 * v + b1 * x1 + b2 * x2 - a1 * y1 - a2 * y2
        y.append(round(out, 4))
        x2 = x1
        x1 = v
        y2 = y1
        y1 = out
    return y

chapters.title: Windows, leakage and spectrum analysis
summary: The DFT assumes the N samples repeat forever. If a sine does not fit a whole number of cycles in the window, the repeat has a jump and energy leaks into many bins.
A window function tapers the signal smoothly to zero at both edges, cutting the leakage at the price of a wider main peak. The Hann window is a popular compromise.
To see how a spectrum changes in time, cut the signal into overlapping frames, window each one and take a DFT of each. The picture of those spectra is a spectrogram.

glossary.def: Spreading of a frequency's energy into neighbouring bins because the window cuts the wave mid-cycle.
A weighting that tapers a frame toward zero at its edges before the DFT.
The window w[n] = 0.5 - 0.5 cos(2 pi n / (N-1)).
Appending zeros before the DFT to get a smoother-looking spectrum.
A plot of spectra over successive frames, showing frequency against time.

keyPoints: Whole cycles in the frame give no leakage.
Better resolution needs a longer frame.
Zero padding does not add information.
Spectrogram = windowed DFTs over time.

items: ELI5. If you cut a note in the middle of a wave, the cut makes a click. Fading the edges in and out hides the click.

Cut a record of a pure tone at a random point and you almost certainly cut the wave mid-cycle. The DFT sees a signal that repeats the chunk end to end, with a sudden jump at the seam. A jump is rich in every frequency, so the clean peak gets skirts of leaked energy.

The remedy is to fade the chunk in and out. A window function multiplies the frame by a smooth hump that starts and ends at zero. The seam disappears and the skirts drop a lot. The cost is a slightly broader peak, because the effective signal is shorter.

Different windows make different trade-offs. The rectangular window, no tapering, has the narrowest peak and the worst leakage. Hann and Hamming reduce leakage a great deal. Blackman reduces it still more with a wider peak. There is no free lunch, only the right compromise for the job.

Resolution is set by the length of the observation. Two tones closer than fs over N cannot be told apart, however much you zero-pad. Padding with zeros only interpolates the same information on a finer grid and makes the plot look smoother.

Real sounds change with time, so we cut the signal into short overlapping frames, window each, take the DFT and stack the magnitudes. The result is the spectrogram: time along one axis, frequency along the other, brightness for strength.
Speech, birdsong and music look like distinctive patterns on it.

    out = []

chapters.title: Applications: noise, pitch, images and compression
summary: The same tools serve many jobs. A median filter erases spikes without blurring edges. Autocorrelation finds the repeat period of a signal, which gives pitch. Decimation lowers the sample rate after low-pass filtering.
An image is a two-dimensional signal; blurring, sharpening and edge detection are 2D convolutions with small kernels.
Compression such as JPEG and MP3 transforms the signal to the frequency domain, discards small or inaudible parts, and stores the rest.

glossary.def: A nonlinear filter that replaces each sample by the median of its neighbourhood.
The similarity of a signal with a delayed copy of itself, as a function of delay.
Lowering the sample rate by keeping every Mth sample after low-pass filtering.
A small grid of weights convolved with an image.
Shifting a signal's frequencies by multiplying it by a carrier wave.

keyPoints: Autocorrelation peak at lag L: period L, pitch fs / L.
Decimate by M: low-pass first, then keep every Mth.
Median kills spikes, mean smears them.
Blur kernel: all positive and sums to 1.
Edge kernel: positive and negative parts.

items: ELI5. Cleaning a noisy sensor, finding the pitch of a voice, blurring a picture and squeezing a song into a small file all use the same tools.

A sensor reading with an occasional wild spike is a headache for averaging, because the spike drags the mean. The median ignores outliers: sort the neighbourhood and take the middle. A three-point median filter removes isolated spikes and keeps sharp steps in place.

How do you find the pitch of a note? Compare the signal with delayed copies of itself. When the delay equals the period, the copy lines up with the original and the match is strong. The first strong peak of this autocorrelation gives the period in samples, and fs divided by that gives the frequency.

To store a signal at a lower rate, you cannot just throw samples away, or high frequencies alias. First low-pass filter to the new Nyquist limit, then keep every Mth sample. Raising the rate, interpolation, works by inserting zeros and then low-pass filtering.

Pictures are signals in two dimensions. Blurring slides a small kernel of positive weights over the image. A kernel with a positive side and a negative side picks out edges. A convolutional neural network is built from layers of such kernels, whose weights are learned rather than designed.

Compression exploits the frequency domain. JPEG cuts an image into small blocks, takes a discrete cosine transform and rounds away the small high-frequency coefficients that the eye barely notices. MP3 does similar things with a model of what the ear cannot hear.
Radio uses modulation to place a message on a carrier frequency so many stations share the air.
